core_insight: A matrix moves the whole plane, and its determinant is the single factor by which it scales every area - negative when it flips the plane over, zero when it squashes the plane flat.
key_ideas: A 2x2 matrix is a linear transformation: it moves every point, keeping grid lines straight, parallel and evenly spaced, and the origin fixed.
The columns of the matrix are where the basis vectors i-hat and j-hat land.
The unit square becomes a parallelogram; its area is the determinant.
Every region scales by the same factor, because any shape can be filled with small grid squares.
det = ad - bc; zero means the plane collapses onto a line, negative means orientation flips.
central_formula: \det\begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix} = ad - bc
intuitions: Stretching a sheet of rubber printed with a grid.
Tracking one tile of the grid is enough to know what happens to all of them.
Turning a sheet of paper over reverses clockwise and counterclockwise.
misconceptions: That the determinant is just an arbitrary formula to memorise.
That different shapes scale by different amounts under the same matrix.
That a negative determinant means negative area.
visual_opportunities: A grid warping under the matrix, with a faint copy of the original behind it.
The basis vectors moving to the matrix columns.
A highlighted unit square turning into a parallelogram with a live area readout.
A circle and a triangle scaling by the same factor.
The whole plane collapsing onto a line; the square flipping over.
